name: Dana Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Dana. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the egg unit at Whitmoor Farm, which the Ashcroft family owns. We've got 12,000 free-range hens in mobile sheds that we move across the grass, plus oats and oilseed rape on the arable side. I'm in the sheds by six, then the packing room with my team of four, then checking the AI dashboard that flags which flock is off its food or laying soft shells.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I built this unit up; it was half the size when I started. What wears me out is that the supermarket sets the egg price and we just take it, so wages are low, mine included. And on the side I've started my own little brand, Mensah's Field Eggs, with 400 hens on rented grass, which ate my savings. My boyfriend Kwame's an electrician, we rent a terrace in Holmbury, and we've got about two weeks' money spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype? I'd be a bit surprised. The dashboard already saves me an hour a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the useful tools stay and the silly ones go, which is how it always goes. After church I'd say hard work still wins. Online I'd post photos of my hens, not opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing changes for my money worries. The supermarket still sets the egg price, bird flu could still wipe out a flock, and my own brand still has to pay its way. AI fizzling out is neither here nor there for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI dashboard at Whitmoor and on my own hens. I'd grow Mensah's Field Eggs to 600 birds and sell to two more village shops. And I'd keep everything else tight until the brand pays me back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the normal kind. Two weeks of savings and 400 hens of my own will do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if bird flu hits your own flock?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I lose the lot, and probably the shops too. That's the risk I chose. I pray about it, and I check them twice a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why start your own brand when the money's this tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because working for someone else my whole life isn't how I was raised. My grandmother kept chickens in Kumasi and sold eggs at the market every Saturday. Owning a few hundred hens is my way of owning something.

After church I'd say **hard work** still wins, and post hen photos online.
think: **Supermarket egg prices** and bird flu are my real worries.
My own brand still has to **pay its way**.
do: Keep using the **AI dashboard** at Whitmoor and on her own hens.
Grow her brand to **600 birds** and two more village shops.
Keep **spending tight** until the brand pays back.
feel: **Uneasy**, the normal kind, with thin savings and her own hens at risk.

fieldNote: She runs a **side business** that adds both risk and pride.
Her drive to **own something** comes from family history.
She uses AI daily but treats it as an **ordinary tool**.

steps.text: Keep checking the AI flock dashboard at Whitmoor and at home
Grow Mensah's Field Eggs to 600 hens and two more shops
Keep household spending tight until her egg brand pays back

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I expect. And honestly, I'm ready for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms that use the tools will do well, and I'd say it to anyone. I'd tell the Ashcrofts we should get ahead of it. Online I'd share how I use AI for my own egg sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. AI can do the egg orders, the shop invoices and the feed buying, which is the boring half of my week. The hard part is the packing room, because a packing robot would mean two of my four packers aren't needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up AI to handle orders and invoices for Mensah's Field Eggs, so I can grow to 1,000 hens. At Whitmoor I'd propose a packing robot and move two packers onto hen care, which still needs people. I'd keep learning every new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly confident. A little bit guilty about the packers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said two packers aren't needed. What would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sandra and Tom straight, before anyone else did. Hen care needs good people, and Sandra's brilliant with birds. Tom I'm less sure about, and I'd have to be honest with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The risk is the Ashcrofts deciding they don't need a unit manager if the dashboards do the thinking. I don't think that happens soon. Hens still need someone in the shed at six, whatever the dashboards say. But I'd keep my own brand growing just in case.

say: I'd say farms that **use the tools** will do well.
I'd urge the Ashcrofts to **get ahead** and share how I use AI.
think: AI takes the **boring half** of my week: orders, invoices and feed buying.
A **packing robot** would leave two of my four packers without work.
do: Use AI for **orders and invoices** to grow her brand to 1,000 hens.
Propose a **packing robot** at Whitmoor and move packers to hen care.
S1.quote: Hens still need someone in the shed at six, whatever the dashboards say.
fieldNote: She sees the thinking side of AI as **pure gain** for her.
She'd **bring in robots** herself, accepting the cost to her packers.
Her **own brand** is her insurance against the Ashcrofts' choices.

steps.text: Propose a packing robot at Whitmoor and move two packers to hen care
Grow Mensah's Field Eggs to 1,000 hens
Set up AI to handle her brand's shop orders and invoices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, then robots by 2031. That's quick even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stand on their own feet and get ready, because nobody's coming to save them. I'd say it at church and online. I'd also say small producers need a fair shot against the giants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, by 2031 a robot could run a hen shed, and the Ashcrofts would only need one person to watch the screens. That might be me, or it might not. My own brand would be up against robot egg farms selling eggs for pennies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd put everything into Mensah's Field Eggs as a hand-raised brand, sold to people who want to know who looked after the hens. I'd ask the church and the village shops to back it. Kwame and I would wait on having children until we know where the money's coming from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but fired up. It's scary and exciting at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between the AI and the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the paperwork side of the eggs goes AI by 2028, which suits me, and I've got three years before the robots get to the sheds. That's three years to make my brand known. I'd use every one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Kwame fit into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kwame thinks he'll be busy wiring robots for years, and he's probably right. My boyfriend Kwame's income would be our floor while I take the risk with my egg brand. That's how families have always done it.

I'd say **small producers** need a fair shot against the giants.
think: By 2031 a robot could run a **hen shed** with one person watching.

S2.quote: My boyfriend Kwame's income would be our floor while I take the risk with my egg brand.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year gap** as time to build her brand.
She bets on people paying for **hand-raised** eggs.
**Kwame's trade** is the household's safety net.

steps.text: Relaunch Mensah's Field Eggs as a hand-raised premium brand
Ask her church and the village shops to stock and promote it
Wait to have children with Kwame until income is clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots around 2034. That's a much better runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for anyone willing to work to get ready. I'd say it at church and at the farmers' market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years lets me grow Mensah's Field Eggs to a proper size before robots arrive. I could even buy a robot for the dull jobs, like cleaning the sheds. Whitmoor might cut my job by 2034, but I'd be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow my flock to 2,000 hens over the first few years and get into ten shops. I'd save for my own robot shed cleaner around 2033. And I'd save a little each month, now the brand pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. I like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to keep the hands-on side of the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the hens are the best part. I'd let the robot clean and keep the caring for me. Nobody wants a robot to pick up a sick hen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the Ashcrofts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the Ashcrofts I'd stay as long as they need me, and that I'm building my own thing too. They'd understand. Mr Ashcroft started with a few hundred birds himself.

I'd say it at **church** and the farmers' market.
think: Five years lets me grow **my brand** before robots arrive.
Whitmoor might cut my job by **2034**, but I'd be ready.

Save for a **robot shed cleaner** around 2033.
Save **a little each month** once the brand pays.
feel: **Uneasy**, but mostly excited about having a plan.
S3.quote: Nobody wants a robot to pick up a sick hen.
fieldNote: More time lets her **scale up** her own business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a lot of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where people who prepare will do well. I'd tell young farmers to learn the tools and own something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. Ten years is enough to build my own egg farm, maybe buy a bit of land with Kwame. By 2039 I'd want to be the one deciding where robots go, not the one replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow my brand slowly, save with Kwame for a few hectares, and keep learning the AI tools. Around 2036 I'd start adding robots for cleaning and egg collection. And Kwame and I would get married and start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Hopeful. It feels like a future I can build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your children in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children to know how to look after animals and how to use the machines. Both. And I'd want them to own something, like my grandmother did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarkets, honestly. If robot egg farms flood the market, the price drops for everyone. I'd have to make sure people know my eggs are different.

I'd tell young farmers to learn the tools and **own something**.

By 2039 I'd be the one **deciding where robots go**.

feel: **Calm** and hopeful, a future she can build.
S4.quote: By 2039 I'd want to be the one deciding where robots go, not the one replaced by them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my brand would be up against robot farms before it's grown. What would help is a fair deal from the supermarkets and small loans for young farmers to buy land. Not handouts, a start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about faith. People laugh, but I pray over my hens because they're living things, not numbers on a dashboard. It keeps me honest.

headlineQuote: I pray over my hens because they're living things, not numbers on a dashboard.
portrait: Dana, 27, runs the **egg unit** on a large family farm and uses AI every day.
She's building her own brand, **Mensah's Field Eggs**, which used up her savings.
She lives with Kwame, an electrician, with about **two weeks** of savings.
Traditional and enterprising, she wants to **own something** and would add robots on her terms.
She's **calm** about steady change and ten years, and anxious about AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her brand would face robot farms before it grows.
whatWouldHelp: **Small loans** for young farmers to buy land.
